prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff ERISA participant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plan administrator's decision is arbitrary and capricious when it relies on a file-only review and disregards treating physicians without explanation.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Administrator's Denial Was Arbitrary and Capricious Because It Rested on a File-Only Review and Ignored the Treating Physicians' Opinions Without Explanation.**

Review of a benefits denial under an arbitrary-and-capricious standard is deferential, but it is not a rubber stamp. "[D]eferential review is not no review." *McDonald v. W.-S. Life Ins. Co.*, 347 F.3d 161, 172 (6th Cir. 2003). A decision survives only if it is "the result of a deliberate, principled reasoning process" and is supported by substantial evidence. *Glenn v. MetLife*, 461 F.3d 660, 666 (6th Cir. 2006), *aff'd sub nom. Metro. Life Ins. Co. v. Glenn*, 554 U.S. 105 (2008). The Sixth Circuit looks closely at how the administrator handled the medical evidence. *See Kalish v. Liberty Mut./Liberty Life Assurance Co. of Bos.*, 419 F.3d 501, 508 (6th Cir. 2005). It also looks closely at whether the administrator's process was thorough. *See Elliott v. Metro. Life Ins. Co.*, 473 F.3d 613, 621 (6th Cir. 2006).

**A. Plan administrators may not arbitrarily disregard treating physicians' opinions.**

Plan administrators need not give treating physicians the special deference that applies in Social Security cases. *Black & Decker Disability Plan v. Nord*, 538 U.S. 822, 834 (2003). But *Nord* also holds that administrators "may not arbitrarily refuse to credit a claimant's reliable evidence, including the opinions of a treating physician." *Id.* The Sixth Circuit applies that limit. An administrator that rejects the conclusions of the physicians who treated the claimant must give a reasoned explanation for doing so. *See Calvert v. Firstar Fin., Inc.*, 409 F.3d 286, 295–97 (6th Cir. 2005); *Kalish*, 419 F.3d at 508–10. Silence is not an explanation. An administrator acts arbitrarily when it ignores or fails to engage with the claimant's medical evidence. *See Moon v. Unum Provident Corp.*, 405 F.3d 373, 379–81 (6th Cir. 2005); *Evans v. UnumProvident Fin. Servs. Grp.*, 434 F.3d 866, 877–78 (6th Cir. 2006).

**B. Reliance on a file-only review undermines the denial, especially when paired with that disregard.**

The Sixth Circuit has held that a file-only review is not improper in itself. *Calvert*, 409 F.3d at 296. But it has repeatedly recognized that relying on a non-examining physician's paper review, to the exclusion of the opinions of physicians who examined the claimant, weighs against the reasonableness of the decision. In *Kalish*, the court found a denial arbitrary where the administrator relied on a file review over the claimant's treating sources. 419 F.3d at 508–10. In *Elliott*, the court explained that a file review "raise[s] questions about the thoroughness and accuracy of the benefits determination," particularly where the plan itself reserved the right to examine the claimant and chose not to. 473 F.3d at 621; *see also Smith v. Cont'l Cas. Co.*, 450 F.3d 253, 263 (6th Cir. 2006). The court reached the same conclusion in *Bennett v. Kemper National Services, Inc.*, 514 F.3d 547, 554 (6th Cir. 2008), where the administrator credited its own reviewers over the claimant's treating sources. And in *Javery v. Lucent Technologies, Inc.*, 741 F.3d 686, 700–01 (6th Cir. 2014), the court scrutinized a decision that depended on records reviewers who never examined the claimant.

The administrator's own financial interest sharpens this scrutiny. An administrator that both decides claims and pays them has a conflict of interest, which courts weigh as a factor. *Glenn*, 461 F.3d at 666–69. That factor carries more weight where, as here, the process favored the payor. The administrator chose reviewers who had never met the claimant. It then adopted their conclusions over those of the treating physicians and did not say why.

**C. Applied here, the denial cannot stand.**

[Plaintiff]'s treating physicians examined [him/her] over time, documented objective findings, and consistently concluded that [he/she] could not perform the duties of [his/her] occupation. The administrator never examined [Plaintiff]. It obtained a file-only review from a physician who saw only paper records. It then adopted that reviewer's conclusions without addressing the treating physicians' findings or explaining why they were less credible. The denial letters do not identify any objective evidence that contradicts the treating physicians. They do not explain why a non-examining reviewer's reading of the record should prevail over the opinions of the doctors who examined [Plaintiff]. And they do not say why the plan declined to use its right to obtain an independent examination. *See Evans*, 434 F.3d at 877–78; *Elliott*, 473 F.3d at 621.

Under *Nord*, *Kalish*, *Calvert*, and *Bennett*, that combination is the kind of unexplained discounting of reliable medical evidence that is arbitrary and capricious. A decision that rests on a one-sided paper review and ignores the treating physicians' opinions is not "the result of a deliberate, principled reasoning process." *Glenn*, 461 F.3d at 666. The Court should reverse the judgment and hold that the denial was arbitrary and capricious.
